claim: Brain organoids have been used to recapitulate the processes of brain development and related diseases.
source: Brain organoids have been used to recapitulate the processes of brain development and related diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of brain organoids, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The lack of vasculatures limits the utility of brain organoids.
source: However, the lack of vasculatures, which regulate neurogenesis and brain disorders, limits the utility of brain organoids.
evidence: This statement is presented as a known limitation in the field.

claim: Vasculatures regulate neurogenesis and brain disorders.
source: However, the lack of vasculatures, which regulate neurogenesis and brain disorders, limits the utility of brain organoids.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the Introduction section.

claim: Vessel and brain organoids were induced separately and then fused together to obtain vascularized brain organoids.
source: In this study, we induced vessel and brain organoids, respectively, and then fused two types of organoids together to obtain vascularized brain organoids.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The fused brain organoids were engrafted with robust vascular network-like structures.
source: The fused brain organoids were engrafted with robust vascular network-like structures and exhibited increased number of neural progenitors, in line with the possibility that vessels regulate neural development.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental observations.

claim: The fused brain organoids exhibited increased number of neural progenitors.
source: The fused brain organoids were engrafted with robust vascular network-like structures and exhibited increased number of neural progenitors, in line with the possibility that vessels regulate neural development.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Fusion organoids contained functional blood–brain barrier-like structures.
source: Fusion organoids also contained functional blood–brain barrier-like structures, as well as microglial cells, a specific population of immune cells in the brain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including immunostaining and permeability assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Fusion organoids contained microglial cells.
source: Fusion organoids also contained functional blood–brain barrier-like structures, as well as microglial cells, a specific population of immune cells in the brain.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and scRNA-seq data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Microglial cells are a specific population of immune cells in the brain.
source: Fusion organoids also contained functional blood–brain barrier-like structures, as well as microglial cells, a specific population of immune cells in the brain.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about microglia.

claim: The incorporated microglia responded actively to immune stimuli.
source: The incorporated microglia responded actively to immune stimuli to the fused brain organoids and showed ability of engulfing synapses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing LPS-induced inflammatory response in Figure 5G.

claim: The incorporated microglia showed ability of engulfing synapses.
source: The incorporated microglia responded actively to immune stimuli to the fused brain organoids and showed ability of engulfing synapses.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing PSD95 puncta within microglia in Figure 5H.

claim: Brain organoids derived from human pluripotent stem cells have been developed to model developmental programs of human fetal brain.
source: Recently, brain organoids (BOrs) derived from human pluripotent stem cells (PSCs), including induced PSCs (iPSCs) and embryonic stem cells (ESCs), have been developed to model developmental programs of human fetal brain, recapitulate developmental, psychiatric, and degenerative brain diseases (Amin and Paşca, 2018; Di Lullo and Kriegstein, 2017; Kelava and Lancaster, 2016; Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Brain organoids have been developed to recapitulate developmental, psychiatric, and degenerative brain diseases.
source: Recently, brain organoids (BOrs) derived from human pluripotent stem cells (PSCs), including induced PSCs (iPSCs) and embryonic stem cells (ESCs), have been developed to model developmental programs of human fetal brain, recapitulate developmental, psychiatric, and degenerative brain diseases (Amin and Paşca, 2018; Di Lullo and Kriegstein, 2017; Kelava and Lancaster, 2016; Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The neurovascular system is required for oxygen and nutrient supply.
source: However, the lack of neurovascular system, which is not only required for oxygen and nutrient supply, but also regulates neurogenesis and brain functions (Delgado et al., 2014; Tata et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2015; Zlokovic, 2011), limits the applications of brain organoids.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The neurovascular system regulates neurogenesis and brain functions.
source: However, the lack of neurovascular system, which is not only required for oxygen and nutrient supply, but also regulates neurogenesis and brain functions (Delgado et al., 2014; Tata et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2015; Zlokovic, 2011), limits the applications of brain organoids.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Vascularization of brain organoids represents one of the most demanded improvements in the field.
source: Thus, vascularization of brain organoids represents one of the most demanded improvements in the field (Di Lullo and Kriegstein, 2017; Giandomenico and Lancaster, 2017; Kelava and Lancaster, 2016; Mansour et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Blood vessels of the vertebrate brain are formed via sequential vasculogenesis and angiogenesis processes.
source: Blood vessels of the vertebrate brain are formed via sequential vasculogenesis and angiogenesis processes, which involve the initial invasion of endothelial cells (ECs) into the neuroepithelium regions via the perivascular plexus, their subsequent coalescence into primitive blood vessels, and growth and remodeling to form a mature vascular network (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Endothelial cells are derived from the mesoderm-derived angioblasts.
source: ECs are derived from the mesoderm-derived angioblasts (Zadeh and Guha, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Endothelial cells can be derived in vitro from human PSCs.
source: It has been shown that ECs can be derived in vitro from human PSCs, and these ECs can be potentially useful in engineering artificial functional blood vessels (Harding et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The generation of complex vascularized organs from PSCs is challenging because it depends on the exquisite orchestration of cues from multiple germ layers.
source: However, the generation of complex vascularized organs from PSCs is still challenging because it depends on the exquisite orchestration of cues from multiple germ layers and the gene expression profiles of ECs are controlled by finely patterned microenvironmental cues during organogenesis (Cleaver and Melton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Wimmer et al. reported the generation of self-organizing human blood vessel organoids induced from PSCs.
source: Recently, Wimmer et al. reported the generation of self-organizing human blood vessel organoids (VOrs) induced from PSCs and the application in the study of diabetic vasculopathy (Wimmer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Endothelial cells have mesodermal origin.
source: Given the mesodermal origin of ECs and ectodermic origin of neural fates (Nostro et al., 2008; Stern, 2005), one barrier for the generation of vascularized BOrs is the difficulty in simultaneous application of induction factors for distinct germ layers and cell fates due to mutual repression.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neural fates have ectodermic origin.
source: Given the mesodermal origin of ECs and ectodermic origin of neural fates (Nostro et al., 2008; Stern, 2005), one barrier for the generation of vascularized BOrs is the difficulty in simultaneous application of induction factors for distinct germ layers and cell fates due to mutual repression.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: One barrier for the generation of vascularized brain organoids is the difficulty in simultaneous application of induction factors for distinct germ layers due to mutual repression.
source: Given the mesodermal origin of ECs and ectodermic origin of neural fates (Nostro et al., 2008; Stern, 2005), one barrier for the generation of vascularized BOrs is the difficulty in simultaneous application of induction factors for distinct germ layers and cell fates due to mutual repression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different germ layer origins and cited work.

claim: Pham et al. attempted to vascularize brain organoids by embedding with iPSCs induced endothelial cells.
source: Since the early attempt to vascularize the BOrs by embedding with iPSCs induced ECs (Pham et al., 2018), several additional strategies have been developed.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Grafted cerebral organoids with host blood vessel invasion exhibited lower cell death rate and enhanced maturation.
source: One strategy took advantage of natural angiogenesis of host blood vessels that sprout and grow into the grafted cerebral organoids, which later exhibited lower cell death rate and enhanced maturation (Mansour et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Transcription factor-mediated differentiation of PSCs into EC-like cells during cerebral organoid induction enhanced the maturation process.
source: Another approach utilized transcription factor-mediated differentiation of a subset of PSCs into EC-like cells during cerebral organoid induction, whose maturation process was also enhanced (Cakir et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: None of the previous methods can form an entirely and integrated vascular network in the cerebral organoids in vitro.
source: Although grafted BOrs appeared to have established functional blood vessels (Mansour et al., 2018), none of these methods can form an entirely and integrated vascular network in the cerebral organoids in vitro.
evidence: This is an assessment of previous methods based on the literature.

claim: Previous brain organoid models lacked functional microglial cells.
source: They all lacked the functional microglial cells, the only lifelong resident immune cells, which are derived from mesodermal origin (Muffat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an assessment of previous methods supported by a citation.

claim: Microglial cells are the only lifelong resident immune cells in the brain.
source: They all lacked the functional microglial cells, the only lifelong resident immune cells, which are derived from mesodermal origin (Muffat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Microglial cells are derived from mesodermal origin.
source: They all lacked the functional microglial cells, the only lifelong resident immune cells, which are derived from mesodermal origin (Muffat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The blood–brain barrier is mainly composed of endothelial cells, astrocytes, and pericytes.
source: In addition, the blood–brain barrier (BBB), the structure mainly composed of ECs, astrocytes, and pericytes, which protects the brain from circulation, is also lacking in the current ectodermal BOr models.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about BBB composition.

claim: The blood–brain barrier protects the brain from circulation.
source: In addition, the blood–brain barrier (BBB), the structure mainly composed of ECs, astrocytes, and pericytes, which protects the brain from circulation, is also lacking in the current ectodermal BOr models.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about BBB function.

claim: BBB spheroids were created by co-culture of primary endothelial cells, pericytes, and astrocytes as an in vitro screening platform for brain-penetrating agents.
source: By co-culture of primary ECs, pericytes, and astrocytes, the BBB spheroids were created as an in vitro screening platform for brain-penetrating agents (Bergmann et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Brain-specific vascular organoids were cultured in medium containing neurotrophic factors at the maturation stage to obtain cerebrovascular characteristics.
source: Here, we develop an induction approach for brain-specific vascular organoids, which were cultured in medium containing neurotrophic factors at the maturation stage, to obtain cerebrovascular characteristics of the VOrs.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: A large number of microglial cells were induced along with other types of vascular cells in the vessel organoids.
source: Interestingly, a large number of microglial cells were induced by this approach along with other types of vascular cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by scRNA-seq and immunostaining data.

claim: The vessel organoids were fused with cerebral organoids in Matrigel, leading to the formation of vascularized brain organoids with invasion of microglia.
source: The VOrs were then fused with the cerebral organoids in the Matrigel, leading to the formation of vascularized BOrs with invasion of microglia, which could be activated upon immune stimuli.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and findings of the study.

claim: Microglia in the fused organoids could be activated upon immune stimuli.
source: The VOrs were then fused with the cerebral organoids in the Matrigel, leading to the formation of vascularized BOrs with invasion of microglia, which could be activated upon immune stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing LPS-induced response in Figure 5G.

claim: The canonical Wnt signaling is required for the development of ESC-derived mesoderm.
source: It has been shown that the canonical Wnt signaling is required for the development of ESC-derived mesoderm (Lindsley et al., 2006) and the activation of Wnt signaling induces the mesoderm differentiation from human PSCs (Nostro et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The activation of Wnt signaling induces mesoderm differentiation from human PSCs.
source: It has been shown that the canonical Wnt signaling is required for the development of ESC-derived mesoderm (Lindsley et al., 2006) and the activation of Wnt signaling induces the mesoderm differentiation from human PSCs (Nostro et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: EC-generating vascular progenitors are derived from mesoderm during embryogenesis.
source: Considering that EC-generating vascular progenitors (VPs) are derived from mesoderm during embryogenesis (Gupta et al., 2006), we performed guided mesodermal induction of H9 human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), followed by endothelial differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: 2-day-old embryonic bodies from hESCs were treated with GSK3 inhibitor CHIR99021 to activate the canonical Wnt signaling for mesoderm induction.
source: First, we treated 2-day-old (D2) embryonic bodies (EBs) from hESCs, which stably expressed GFP, with GSK3 inhibitor CHIR99021 to activate the canonical Wnt signaling for mesoderm induction (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: bFGF, VEGF, and BMP4 have been shown to promote vascular progenitor differentiation into endothelial cells.
source: After 2 days, the EBs were treated with basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4), all of which have been shown to be able to promote VP differentiation into ECs (Cai et al., 2012; Jih et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Vessel-like structures sprouted out from the spheroids at day 16.
source: Notably, vessel-like structures sprouted out from the spheroids at day 16 (D16) (Figure 1B), reminiscent of initial vasculogenesis and angiogenesis.
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The vessel organoids showed gradual increase in size during the maturation stage after day 16.
source: Remarkably, the VOrs showed gradual increase in the size during the maturation stage after day 16 (D16), with apparent tubular network characteristics at D20 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The vessel organoids exhibited apparent tubular network characteristics at D20.
source: Remarkably, the VOrs showed gradual increase in the size during the maturation stage after day 16 (D16), with apparent tubular network characteristics at D20 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At D40, the vessel organoid gradually formed into a sphere with smooth edges due to Matrigel's wrapping.
source: At D40, the VOr gradually formed into a sphere with smooth edges due to Matrigel's wrapping, and its internal blood vessel structures developed more dense and integrated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The internal blood vessel structures of vessel organoids developed more dense and integrated at D40.
source: At D40, the VOr gradually formed into a sphere with smooth edges due to Matrigel's wrapping, and its internal blood vessel structures developed more dense and integrated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The stemness markers NANOG and OCT4 showed marked decrease 2 days upon mesoderm induction.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, the stemness markers (NANOG, OCT4) showed marked decrease 2 days upon mesoderm induction (D4), whereas the vessel markers (PECAM1, VE-cadherin, VWF, VEGFR1, VEGFR2, and PDGFRβ) markedly increased after VP differentiation (D7 and thereafter).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The vessel markers PECAM1, VE-cadherin, VWF, VEGFR1, VEGFR2, and PDGFRβ markedly increased after vascular progenitor differentiation.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, the stemness markers (NANOG, OCT4) showed marked decrease 2 days upon mesoderm induction (D4), whereas the vessel markers (PECAM1, VE-cadherin, VWF, VEGFR1, VEGFR2, and PDGFRβ) markedly increased after VP differentiation (D7 and thereafter).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Flow cytometry results revealed the appearance of GFP+CD31+ endothelial cells after D7.
source: In line with this, flow cytometry results revealed the appearance of GFP+CD31+ ECs after D7, indicating the induction of the ECs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CD31+ endothelial cells in vessel organoids at D40 showed integrated and complex structures.
source: Morphologically, CD31+ ECs in VOrs at D40 showed integrated and complex structures (Figure 1D) and exhibited remarkable vascular branches and tips undergoing angiogenesis-like processes (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Endothelial cells in vessel organoids exhibited remarkable vascular branches and tips undergoing angiogenesis-like processes.
source: Morphologically, CD31+ ECs in VOrs at D40 showed integrated and complex structures (Figure 1D) and exhibited remarkable vascular branches and tips undergoing angiogenesis-like processes (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The 3D-reconstructed cross-section revealed tubular structures in vessel organoids, reminiscent of vessel lumen.
source: The 3D-reconstructed cross-section revealed tubular structures in VOrs, reminiscent of vessel lumen (Figure 1E, see top right e1).
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction imaging shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Hydraulic pressure caused liquid flow and vessel wall expansion without leakage in vessel organoids.
source: To determine the connectivity and integrity of vessel-like structures, we injected fluid into the lumens and observed that the hydraulic pressure caused liquid flow and vessel wall expansion without leakage (see Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by video data showing fluid injection experiment.

claim: PDGFRβ-labeled pericytes were observed in close contact with endothelial cells undergoing vessel differentiation.
source: Notably, PDGFRβ-labeled pericytes that are believed to regulate EC maturation, stabilize vessel wall, and control angiogenesis were also observed in close contact with ECs undergoing vessel differentiation (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Pericytes regulate endothelial cell maturation, stabilize vessel wall, and control angiogenesis.
source: Notably, PDGFRβ-labeled pericytes that are believed to regulate EC maturation, stabilize vessel wall, and control angiogenesis were also observed in close contact with ECs undergoing vessel differentiation (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about pericyte function.

claim: The average vessel length in vessel organoids was around 400 mm.
source: The average vessel length was around 400 mm, the vessel lacunarity was 0.15, and the total number of junctions was about 700–800 per VOr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The vessel lacunarity in vessel organoids was 0.15.
source: The average vessel length was around 400 mm, the vessel lacunarity was 0.15, and the total number of junctions was about 700–800 per VOr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The total number of junctions in vessel organoids was about 700–800 per organoid.
source: The average vessel length was around 400 mm, the vessel lacunarity was 0.15, and the total number of junctions was about 700–800 per VOr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Vessel organoids after D14 had the ability of uptaking DiI-Ac-LDL.
source: We found that VOrs after D14 already had the ability of uptaking DiI-Ac-LDL, whereas ESCs could not (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by DiI-Ac-LDL uptake assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ESCs could not uptake DiI-Ac-LDL.
source: We found that VOrs after D14 already had the ability of uptaking DiI-Ac-LDL, whereas ESCs could not (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by DiI-Ac-LDL uptake assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing of vessel organoids at D40 analyzed transcriptome of about 7000 single cells.
source: To investigate the fidelity of VOrs in recapitulating the cerebrovascular cell types, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of VOrs at D40 using 10x Genomic chromium system (Macosko et al., 2015; Zilionis et al., 2017). After the quality control data filtering, we analyzed transcriptome of about 7000 single cells, with 200–7000 genes detected per cell and the mitochondrial gene ratio under 5%.
evidence: This describes the scRNA-seq experiment performed in the study.

claim: The cells in vessel organoids were clustered into nine main cell types including fibroblast, pericyte, proliferative vascular progenitor, endothelial cell, smooth muscle cell, microglia, immune cell, and unknown cluster.
source: According to cell-type markers of the mice brain vessels identified by single-cell sequencing (He et al., 2018; Vanlandewijck et al., 2018), the cells in VOrs were clustered into nine main cell types (Figure 2A), including fibroblast (FB), pericyte (PC), proliferative vascular progenitor (MKI67+ VP), EC, smooth muscle cell (SMC), microglia (MG), immune cell (IM), and unknown cluster (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Fibroblast accounted for the highest proportion of total cells in vessel organoids.
source: FB accounted for the highest proportion of total cells and MG the lowest (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Microglia accounted for the lowest proportion of total cells in vessel organoids.
source: FB accounted for the highest proportion of total cells and MG the lowest (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The vasculatures in vessel organoids exhibited positive signals of the smooth muscle cell marker αSMA.
source: Immunostaining showed that the vasculatures in VOrs exhibited positive signals of the SMC marker αSMA, the pericyte marker PDGFRβ, and the EC marker CD31 (Figure 2D and E), confirming the results obtained using scRNA-seq.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The vasculatures in vessel organoids exhibited positive signals of the pericyte marker PDGFRβ.
source: Immunostaining showed that the vasculatures in VOrs exhibited positive signals of the SMC marker αSMA, the pericyte marker PDGFRβ, and the EC marker CD31 (Figure 2D and E), confirming the results obtained using scRNA-seq.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The vasculatures in vessel organoids exhibited positive signals of the endothelial cell marker CD31.
source: Immunostaining showed that the vasculatures in VOrs exhibited positive signals of the SMC marker αSMA, the pericyte marker PDGFRβ, and the EC marker CD31 (Figure 2D and E), confirming the results obtained using scRNA-seq.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: The presence of microglia-like cells was verified by staining with specific markers IBA1, TREM2, and TMEM119 in D40 vessel organoids.
source: Meanwhile, the presence of MG-like cells was verified by the staining with specific markers IBA1, TREM2, and TMEM119, together with CD31 labeling for ECs in D40 VOrs (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: DLL4 and EPHB4 mark the venous and arterial endothelial cells, respectively.
source: Interestingly, DLL4 and EPHB4, which mark the venous and arterial ECs, respectively (Vanlandewijck et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018), were found to express only in separate EC populations (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DLL4 and EPHB4 were found to express only in separate endothelial cell populations in vessel organoids.
source: Interestingly, DLL4 and EPHB4, which mark the venous and arterial ECs, respectively (Vanlandewijck et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018), were found to express only in separate EC populations (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2G and 2H.

claim: Endothelial cells in vessel organoids underwent spontaneous functional maturation.
source: This result indicates that ECs in VOrs already underwent spontaneous functional maturation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of arterial and venous markers in separate EC populations.

claim: Immunostaining confirmed the presence of venous and arterial endothelial cell subtypes in vessel organoids.
source: Immunostaining also confirmed the presence of the venous and arterial EC subtypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Fibroblast and pericyte were among the early developed cell types in vessel organoids.
source: Then, we used a panel of markers to annotate the main cell types and found that FB and PC were among the early developed cell types while the EC and MG were among the later ones (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Endothelial cells and microglia were among the later developed cell types in vessel organoids.
source: Then, we used a panel of markers to annotate the main cell types and found that FB and PC were among the early developed cell types while the EC and MG were among the later ones (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: Pericytes appeared earlier than smooth muscle cells in vessel organoid development.
source: Using the developmental trajectory analysis, we found that PC appeared earlier than SMC (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Pericyte markers MEF2C, PDGFRβ, and RGS5 were highly expressed in the early stages but downregulated in the later stages.
source: PC markers (MEF2C, PEGFRβ, RGS5) were highly expressed in the early stages but downregulated in the later stages, while SMC markers (ACTA2, MYL9, TAGLN) showed opposite tendency (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Smooth muscle cell markers ACTA2, MYL9, and TAGLN showed opposite tendency to pericyte markers, being upregulated in later stages.
source: PC markers (MEF2C, PEGFRβ, RGS5) were highly expressed in the early stages but downregulated in the later stages, while SMC markers (ACTA2, MYL9, TAGLN) showed opposite tendency (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The molecular features of the five major cell types in vessel organoids were similar to the counterparts of mouse cerebrovascular system.
source: First, we compared the VOrs and mouse cerebrovascular scRNA-seq data (He et al., 2018; Vanlandewijck et al., 2018) and found that the molecular features of the five major cell types, including FB, SMC, PC, EC, and MG, in VOrs were similar to the counterparts of mouse cerebrovascular system (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Vessel organoids and human samples showed stronger correlation in endothelial cell and pericyte clusters compared to mouse samples.
source: We analyzed the correlation of these three clusters in VOrs, mouse, and human samples together and found that VOrs and human showed stronger correlation in EC and PC clusters, while MG showed the highest consistency across all three datasets (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Microglia showed the highest consistency across vessel organoid, mouse, and human datasets.
source: We analyzed the correlation of these three clusters in VOrs, mouse, and human samples together and found that VOrs and human showed stronger correlation in EC and PC clusters, while MG showed the highest consistency across all three datasets (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Most of the top differentially expressed genes between vessel organoids and mouse groups showed similar tendency in human samples.
source: Remarkably, most of the top DEGs between VOrs and mouse groups showed similar tendency in human samples (Figure 3I), suggesting the high similarity of ECs in VOrs compared to that in human samples in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The shared differentially expressed genes between vessel organoid vs. mouse and human vs. mouse pairs were related to the angiogenesis pathway.
source: The Gene Ontology (GO) analysis showed that the shared DEGs between VOr vs. mouse and human vs. mouse pairs were related to the angiogenesis pathway, suggesting that human vascular development may be more complex and robust than that of mouse (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Human vascular development may be more complex and robust than that of mouse.
source: The Gene Ontology (GO) analysis showed that the shared DEGs between VOr vs. mouse and human vs. mouse pairs were related to the angiogenesis pathway, suggesting that human vascular development may be more complex and robust than that of mouse (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the GO analysis results.

claim: Marker genes of vessel organoids were highly expressed in the same cell types of human samples.
source: As shown in Figure 3K, marker genes of VOrs were also highly expressed in the same cell types of human samples, further indicating the similarity of corresponding cell type.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Endothelial cells in vessel organoids showed a clear disparity from neuroectodermal epithelial lineage-induced brain microvascular endothelial cells but higher similarity to endothelial cell lineage.
source: We performed principal component analysis (PCA) for ECs in VOrs and other 28 datasets from this study, including the primary ECs, induced ECs (iEC), and Epi-iBMECs, and found that ECs in VOrs showed a clear disparity from Epi-iBMECs but higher similarity to EC lineage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Vessel organoids exhibited strong endothelial cell properties.
source: The top and bottom loading genes showed separate endothelial and epithelial cell-type identities in these datasets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G) and VOrs exhibited strong EC properties (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Two vascular progenitor bodies were put on both sides of one neuroepithelium body for better invasion of vessels into the developing brain organoids.
source: For better invasion of vessels into the developing BOrs, we put two VP bodies in both sides of one NE body (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Vessel organoids labeled by GFP gradually wrapped brain organoids and formed fused vasculature and brain organoids by D40.
source: After co-culture for different days, VOrs labeled by GFP gradually wrapped BOrs and finally formed a fused vasculature and brain organoids (fVBOrs) by D40 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DCX-labeled neurons were enwrapped by invaded vessels labeled by CD31 in fused vasculature and brain organoids.
source: Whole-mount staining of the fVBOrs showed that DCX-labeled neurons were enwrapped by invaded vessels labeled by CD31 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Stronger CLDN5 signals were observed in brain organoid regions in contact with vessels, suggesting the appearance of tight junctions-like structures.
source: Notably, stronger CLDN5 signals were observed in BOr regions in contact with vessels, suggesting the appearance of tight junctions-like structures (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Astrocyte-like cells labeled by S100 or GFAP were observed in fusion organoids, forming neurovascular unit-like structures.
source: Furthermore, astrocyte-like cells labeled by S100 or GFAP were also observed in fusion organoids, forming neurovascular unit-like structures composed of CD31/GFP-labeled vascular structures and MAP2-labeled neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The presence of neurovascular unit structure in fusion organoids was confirmed by transmission electronic microscopy.
source: The presence of neurovascular unit structure in fusion organoids was also confirmed by transmission electronic microscopy (TEM), which showed the EC basement membrane enclosed by pericytes and tightly contacted by end feet of astrocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Angiopep-2 exhibited strong signals in the fused vasculature and brain organoids.
source: We found that Angiopep-2 exhibited strong signals in the fVBOrs, but scrambled peptides displayed no detectable signal (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Scrambled peptides displayed no detectable signal in fused vasculature and brain organoids.
source: We found that Angiopep-2 exhibited strong signals in the fVBOrs, but scrambled peptides displayed no detectable signal (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The intensity of Angiopep-2 signals decreased from the surface to the inner of fused vasculature and brain organoids.
source: The z-stack images showed that the intensity of Angiopep-2 signals decreased from the surface to the inner of fVBOrs (Figure 4F, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by z-stack imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Brain organoids alone showed much weaker Angiopep-2 signals compared to fusion organoids.
source: In contrast to fusion organoids, the BOrs alone showed much weaker Angiopep-2 signals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by comparative permeability assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F and G.

claim: Fused vasculature and brain organoids have developed blood–brain barrier structures with selective permeability.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that fVBOrs have developed BBB structures with selective permeability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results including tight junction markers and permeability assays.

claim: Microglia are developed from the yolk-sac progenitors, which then populate in the developing brain to regulate neurogenesis and neural circuit refinement.
source: It is generally believed that MGs are developed from the yolk-sac progenitors, which then populate in the developing brain to regulate neurogenesis and neural circuit refinement (Kaur et al., 2017; Mosser et al., 2017; Salter and Stevens, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In unguided cerebral organoids, spontaneous microglia can emerge, probably due to the presence of residue mesodermal progenitors.
source: Indeed, in the unguided cerebral organoids, spontaneous MG can emerge (Ormel et al., 2018), probably due to the presence of residue mesodermal progenitors (Quadrato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The expression of microglia marker genes AIF1 and TMEM119 gradually increased during vessel organoid culture.
source: During the VOr culture, the expression of MG marker genes, such as AIF1 or TMEM119, gradually increased (Figure 5C), indicating again the MG induction.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: D40 vessel organoids exhibited increased abundance of microglia with amoeboid-like morphology compared to D25 microglia mostly with round morphology.
source: In line with this notion, D40 VOrs exhibited increased abundance of MG with amoeboid-like morphology compared to D25 MG mostly with round morphology (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Large amount of IBA1+GFP+ microglia-like cells were found in the neural part of fused vasculature and brain organoids.
source: We found large amount of IBA1+GFP+ MG-like cells in the neural part of fVBOrs, whereas BOrs alone had no MG-like signal (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Brain organoids alone had no microglia-like signal.
source: We found large amount of IBA1+GFP+ MG-like cells in the neural part of fVBOrs, whereas BOrs alone had no MG-like signal (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: There were a number of IBA1+GFP- cells in fused vasculature and brain organoids.
source: Notably, there were a number of IBA1+GFP- cells in fVBOrs (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: VEGFR1 is highly expressed in human microglia.
source: Based on the brain RNA-seq database of various cell types in mouse and human (Zhang et al., 2014), VEGFR1 (encoded by FLT1 gene) is highly expressed in human microglia (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published RNA-seq database.

claim: The residue microglia in brain organoids may sense signals such as VEGF from the invading vessels to be motivated and activated.
source: It remains possible that the residue microglia in BOrs sense the signals, such as VEGF, from the invading vessels to be motivated and activated.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of microglia activation.

claim: Treatment with 2 μM PLX5622 for 7 days almost completely eliminated IBA1-labeled cells in vessel organoids.
source: After treatment for 7 days with 2 μM PLX5622, the IBA1-labeled cells were almost completely gone, and the ablation effect lasted for at least 3 days in the absence of PLX5622 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The ablation effect of PLX5622 on microglia lasted for at least 3 days in the absence of PLX5622.
source: After treatment for 7 days with 2 μM PLX5622, the IBA1-labeled cells were almost completely gone, and the ablation effect lasted for at least 3 days in the absence of PLX5622 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: PLX5622 treatment depleted microglia-like cells in D40 fused vasculature and brain organoids.
source: Likewise, the PLX5622 treatment also depleted MG-like cells in D40 fVBOrs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: LPS stimulation caused marked increase in the expression of inflammatory factors TNFα and IL-6 in fused vasculature and brain organoids.
source: The LPS stimulation caused marked increase in the expression of inflammatory factors TNFα and IL-6 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The expression levels of TNFα and IL-6 were attenuated in PLX5622-treated fusion organoids.
source: Interestingly, the expression levels of TNFα or IL-6 were attenuated in PLX5622-treated fusion organoids (Figure 5G), suggesting the involvement of MG-like cells in LPS-induced immune response.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Microglia-like cells are involved in LPS-induced immune response in fusion organoids.
source: Interestingly, the expression levels of TNFα or IL-6 were attenuated in PLX5622-treated fusion organoids (Figure 5G), suggesting the involvement of MG-like cells in LPS-induced immune response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the attenuation of inflammatory response upon microglia depletion.

claim: Microglia play important roles in synapse elimination by engulfing synapses and promote the process of neuronal maturation.
source: MGs also play important roles in synapse elimination by engulfing synapses and promote the process of neuronal maturation (Eroglu and Barres, 2010; Filipello et al., 2018; Gunner et al., 2019; Popova et al., 2021; Schafer et al., 2012; Scott-Hewitt et al., 2020; Zuchero and Barres, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Many PSD95-labeled puncta were distributed within microglia-like cells, indicating synaptic engulfment.
source: Remarkably, many PSD95-labeled puncta were distributed within MG-like cells, indicating synaptic engulfment (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents in fused vasculature and brain organoids significantly decreased.
source: We found that the frequency of spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents (sEPSCs) in fVBOrs significantly decreased, while the amplitude of sEPSC markedly increased (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The amplitude of spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents in fused vasculature and brain organoids markedly increased.
source: We found that the frequency of spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents (sEPSCs) in fVBOrs significantly decreased, while the amplitude of sEPSC markedly increased (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The neurons in fused vasculature and brain organoids exhibited increased inward current amplitudes when clamped at 50 and 60 mV voltage.
source: The neurons in fVBOrs also exhibited increased inward current amplitudes when clamped at 50 and 60 mV voltage, indicating the promoted neuronal excitability in fVBOrs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Neurons in fused vasculature and brain organoids exhibited accelerated functional maturation process.
source: Thus, neurons in fVBOrs exhibited accelerated functional maturation process, largely owing to the integration of vasculature and/or MG-like cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on electrophysiology data and is attributed to vasculature and/or microglia integration.

claim: Vasculature acts as a critical niche that helps maintain the survival and stemness of neural progenitors.
source: It has been shown that vasculature acts as a critical niche that helps maintain the survival and stemness of neural progenitors, and EC-derived soluble factors might contribute to this function (Delgado et al., 2014; Ottone et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Endothelial cell-derived soluble factors might contribute to maintaining the survival and stemness of neural progenitors.
source: It has been shown that vasculature acts as a critical niche that helps maintain the survival and stemness of neural progenitors, and EC-derived soluble factors might contribute to this function (Delgado et al., 2014; Ottone et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The fused vasculature and brain organoids exhibited marked increase in the thickness of neuroepithelium rosettes compared to brain organoids at the same stages.
source: Interestingly, the fVBOrs exhibited marked increase in the thickness of NE rosettes compared to BOrs at the same corresponding stages (D25) (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The density of neural progenitors marked by PAX6 increased in fusion organoids.
source: In line with this notion, the density of neural progenitors (NP) marked by PAX6 or mitotic NPs marked by p-VIM also increased in fusion organoids (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The density of mitotic neural progenitors marked by p-VIM increased in fusion organoids.
source: In line with this notion, the density of neural progenitors (NP) marked by PAX6 or mitotic NPs marked by p-VIM also increased in fusion organoids (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The density of DCX-labeled differentiated neurons had no difference between fusion organoids and brain organoids during the observation period.
source: However, the density of DCX-labeled differentiated neurons or TBR1-labeled early-born cortical neurons had no difference during the observation period (Figure 6F and G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: The density of TBR1-labeled early-born cortical neurons had no difference between fusion organoids and brain organoids during the observation period.
source: However, the density of DCX-labeled differentiated neurons or TBR1-labeled early-born cortical neurons had no difference during the observation period (Figure 6F and G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The factors produced by vessel organoids might promote the proliferation of neural progenitors after fusion with brain organoids, with little effect on neuronal differentiation.
source: These results suggest that the factors produced by VOrs might promote the proliferation of NPs after fusion with BOrs, with little effect on neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed increase in neural progenitors without change in differentiated neurons.

claim: Brain organoids at D40 or D70 showed abundant apoptotic cells expressing cleaved caspase 3 in the central regions.
source: In line with this notion, BOrs at D40 or D70 showed abundant apoptotic cells expressing cleaved caspase 3 (c-CASP3) in the central regions, whereas the apoptotic cells were markedly reduced in fVBOrs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: The apoptotic cells were markedly reduced in fused vasculature and brain organoids compared to brain organoids alone.
source: In line with this notion, BOrs at D40 or D70 showed abundant apoptotic cells expressing cleaved caspase 3 (c-CASP3) in the central regions, whereas the apoptotic cells were markedly reduced in fVBOrs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: The vessels in fused vasculature and brain organoids may protect neural cells from cell death.
source: This result indicates that the vessels in fVBOrs may protect neural cells from cell death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced apoptosis in fusion organoids.

claim: The diffusion of oxygen by vascular structures or some protective factors secreted by vascular cells may contribute to protecting neural cells from death.
source: The diffusion of oxygen by vascular structures or some protective factors secreted by vascular cells may contribute to this role.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of neuroprotection by vasculature.

claim: The fusion organoids can be used to study interactions among multiple cell types during brain development.
source: Thus, the fusion organoids generated in this work can be used to study interactions among multiple cell types during brain development.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the fusion organoid model.

claim: In vessel organoids only vasculatures close to or located in the brain organoids expressed tight junction markers including CLDN5 and ZO-1.
source: Notably, we found that in fVBOrs only vasculatures close to or located in the BOrs expressed tight junction markers, including CLDN5 and ZO-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C), consistent with the idea that BBB maturation is regulated by neural cues (Lippmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Blood–brain barrier maturation is regulated by neural cues.
source: Notably, we found that in fVBOrs only vasculatures close to or located in the BOrs expressed tight junction markers, including CLDN5 and ZO-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C), consistent with the idea that BBB maturation is regulated by neural cues (Lippmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The reduction in apoptotic cells was also seen in grafted brain organoids with the invasion of host blood vessels.
source: The reduction in apoptotic cells was also seen in grafted BOrs with the invasion of host blood vessels (Mansour et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The vascularized brain organoids may provide a feasible platform for the study of human brain development, vasculature-related diseases, or pharmaceutical interventions that need to pass the blood–brain barrier.
source: It is conceivable that the vascularized BOrs developed in this study may provide a feasible platform for the study of human brain development, vasculature-related diseases, or pharmaceutical interventions, which need to pass the BBB.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential applications of the model.

claim: The vessel organoid model showed intense vascular network with characteristics and specificity of human cerebral vessels based on transcriptomic analysis and functional assay.
source: The vessel organoid model we have established showed intense vascular network with characteristics and specificity of human cerebral vessels based on transcriptomic analysis and functional assay.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from scRNA-seq and functional assays.

claim: The combination of PSC-derived tissue-specific progenitors with endothelial cells and mesenchymal stem cells can generate vascularized organs.
source: It has been demonstrated that the combination of PSC-derived tissue-specific progenitors or relevant tissue samples with ECs and mesenchymal stem cells can generate vascularized organs (Takebe et al., 2015; Takebe et al., 2013), but different derivation of vascular ECs and the brain from distinct germ layers limits the vascularization in BOrs initialized from neuroectoderm induction.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Different derivation of vascular endothelial cells and the brain from distinct germ layers limits the vascularization in brain organoids initialized from neuroectoderm induction.
source: It has been demonstrated that the combination of PSC-derived tissue-specific progenitors or relevant tissue samples with ECs and mesenchymal stem cells can generate vascularized organs (Takebe et al., 2015; Takebe et al., 2013), but different derivation of vascular ECs and the brain from distinct germ layers limits the vascularization in BOrs initialized from neuroectoderm induction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different germ layer origins.

claim: The fused vasculature and brain organoid model lacks active blood flow.
source: Although the fVBOr model has shown branched vessels, it still lacks active blood flow.
evidence: This is an acknowledged limitation of the current model.

claim: Combining microfluidic techniques and organoid cultures to make an 'organ-on-a-chip' may authentically mimic the vascular environment.
source: One possible approach to solve the problem is to combine microfluidic techniques and organoid cultures and make an 'organ-on-a-chip,' which may authentically mimic the vascular environment.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential future approach.

claim: The functional perfusion of vessels in fused vasculature and brain organoids can be verified via in vivo grafting that allows integration of vessels between organoids and the hosts.
source: In further study, the functional perfusion of vessels in fVBOrs can be verified via in vivo grafting that allows integration of vessels between organoids and the hosts as that done in other studies (Pham et al., 2018; Cakir et al., 2019; Cakir et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Blood vessels in the brain are involved in regulating neurogenesis.
source: The blood vessels in the brain are not only required for oxygen and nutrient supply, but also involved in regulating neurogenesis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: The fusion organoids allow for recapitulating early developmental processes like vasculogenesis and angiogenesis.
source: The fusion organoids allow for recapitulating early developmental processes like vasculogenesis and angiogenesis, as well as the integration of microglia.
evidence: This is a summary of the capabilities of the fusion organoid model.

claim: The fusion organoids allow for the integration of microglia.
source: The fusion organoids allow for recapitulating early developmental processes like vasculogenesis and angiogenesis, as well as the integration of microglia.
evidence: This is a summary of the capabilities of the fusion organoid model.

claim: The blood–brain barrier-like structures generated in this study were directly induced from PSCs, which resembled the developmental processes in vivo.
source: Unlike BBB-like structures generated in other studies that combined various mature cell types (Cho et al., 2017; Lippmann et al., 2012; Qian et al., 2017), the ones generated in our study were directly induced from PSCs, which resembled the developmental processes in vivo.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies and a claim about the developmental relevance of the model.

claim: The factors that defined the identity of microglia cells in vessel organoids are not clear.
source: Although the factors that defined the identity of microglia cells in VOrs are not clear, their migration into the BOrs resembled the extra-embryonic originality.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in understanding the mechanism of microglia induction.

claim: The migration of microglia into brain organoids resembled the extra-embryonic originality.
source: Although the factors that defined the identity of microglia cells in VOrs are not clear, their migration into the BOrs resembled the extra-embryonic originality.
evidence: This is an inference about the developmental relevance of microglia migration in the model.

claim: Astrocytes are essential components of the neurovascular units.
source: It is known that astrocytes are essential components of the neurovascular units (Abbott et al., 2006), and their involvement in the maturation of BBB-like units or immune surveillance awaits further investigation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The involvement of astrocytes in the maturation of blood–brain barrier-like units or immune surveillance awaits further investigation.
source: It is known that astrocytes are essential components of the neurovascular units (Abbott et al., 2006), and their involvement in the maturation of BBB-like units or immune surveillance awaits further investigation.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation and suggests future research directions.
